props.title: The Dark Half
props.initialSlug: When The Dark Half Comes To Life

sections.content: The Dark Half (1993) represents one of George A. Romero's most intriguing adaptations of Stephen King's work, diving deep into the psychological horror of a writer's alter ego come to life. Like Secret Window (2004) and Misery (1990), it explores the dark side of authorship, but with a supernatural twist that echoes King's own experience writing under the pseudonym Richard Bachman. The film follows Thad Beaumont, a literary author who "kills off" his more successful pen name George Stark, only to have this darker half manifest physically and embark on a murderous rampage.

sections.content: The film taps into a rich vein of horror movies about writers, including 1408 (2007) and In the Mouth of Madness (1994), where the line between fiction and reality becomes dangerously blurred. Timothy Hutton's dual performance as both Beaumont and Stark creates a compelling Jekyll-and-Hyde dynamic that elevates the material beyond typical horror fare. Romero's direction brings his trademark social commentary, suggesting that creative expression has its own dark price.

The sparrows imagery throughout The Dark Half connects to larger themes in King's work, particularly in The Dark Tower series (2017) and IT (1990), where seemingly innocent elements of nature become harbingers of supernatural doom. The film's exploration of duality predates later psychological horror films like Black Swan (2010) and Identity (2003), which similarly deal with fractured personalities and creative obsession. SUBHEAD: The Writer as Horror Subject

movies.slug: A skeptical author who debunks supernatural occurrences finds himself trapped in a genuinely haunted hotel room.

sections.content: The film stands as part of a significant subset of horror focusing on writers and their creative process, alongside works like Adaptation (2002) and Barton Fink (1991). These films often blur the line between creator and creation, suggesting that the act of writing itself can be a form of psychological horror. Romero's adaptation particularly excels in visualizing the internal struggle of creative identity, making literal the metaphorical battle between commercial success and artistic integrity.
